data.title: Spanberger announces tightened data center restrictions, clean energy mandates in Virginia
data.description:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) on Friday announced a new proposal to tighten restrictions on data center developments in the state. 

The governor’s “Data Center Accountability Framework” outlines several objectives for the commonwealth’s approach to these projects, including cutting down on noise pollution and water use tied to these projects and promoting clean energy and boosting local jobs. 

Spanberger signed an executive order establishing a “rapid-response” AI task force and directing the commonwealth’s chief energy officer to publish a toolkit to help local communities navigate proposed data center projects. 

Additionally, Spanberger’s directive bans state agencies and employees from entering into nondisclosure agreements that keep any information about these planned developments secret. 

The governor expressed her commitment to work with Virginia’s General Assembly to pass legislation aligned with the rest of this framework’s goals.

“The legislature has done so much to raise this issue in the last few months, and I look forward to working with them to codify parts of this plan into Virginia law,” Spanberger said in a Friday statement. 

“At the end of the day, we all want the same thing: we want Virginia to be a national leader in data center accountability,” the moderate Democratic official continued. 

The new Virginia framework follows recent pushes from other governors to place restrictions on data centers in their states. 

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) also signed an executive order on Friday that seeks to stop data center costs from being passed on to local communities as he faces a tight reelection contest against state Attorney General Aaron Ford (D). 

On Thursday, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said he would “absolutely sign” a moratorium on new data center construction projects in his state. Deb Haaland, the Democratic candidate in New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, also supported a similar push this week. 

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who is running for reelection, directed the state’s water development board this week to penalize new data centers that fail to meet water use requirements. 

“Data centers must share the duty to protect Texas water,” the incumbent governor said in a statement announcing this directive. 

Northern Virginia has seen a surge in new data center construction projects, with the region being dubbed “Data Center Alley” because of the sheer number of centers in the area.

Nicole Riley, the director of Virginia governmental affairs for the Data Center Coalition, a trade association representing industry members, expressed the group’s commitment to working with state lawmakers “to ensure workable, balanced policies” in a Friday statement following Spanberger’s announcement. 

“If done right, there is a path for continued job creation, responsible investment, and clean energy deployment that protects ratepayers and delivers benefits for families and communities,” Riley said. 

“However, significant and abrupt policy changes without meaningful stakeholder engagement could prove unworkable and jeopardize the real tangible benefits this industry can create,” the director continued. “We hope the implementation of this process will be based in fact and evidence, and account for the tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity connected to digital infrastructure.”

data.title: Trump says CNN, MS NOW, Politico banned from White House
data.description:
President Trump on Friday said he was banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, a move sure to draw fierce pushback from D.C.’s press corps.

Trump said in a Truth Social post that the ban would be “effective immediately” for those outlets, “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” He suggested more outlets would be banned in the future.

He called CNN “fake news,” and targeted MSNOW, saying the outlet changed its name over “lack of viewership and credibility.”

He also railed against the $8 million the government pays for Politico Pro subscriptions, calling it “illegal and ridiculous.”

“An All Time Record, directly from the United States Government, under Crooked Joe Biden, in order to keep them ‘alive,’ Seems like corruption to me!),” he wrote.

The Hill reached out to all three outlets for comment.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he continued. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Trump has tried to ban outlets from White House coverage before. Last year, he barred The Associated Press and excluded The Wall Street Journal from traveling in the press pool.

DEVELOPING …

data.title: Texas agency suspends Flock camera approvals
data.description:
The Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) suspended issuing approvals for Flock’s automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras amid growing security and privacy concerns surrounding the technology.

“TxDOT’s role is to review permits to ensure license plate readers are installed correctly and safely along state-owned roadways,” an agency spokesperson told NewsNation in a statement. “TxDOT does not have access to the data collected from the license plate readers, and these cameras are placed at the request of law enforcement.”

“Under the direction of Governor Greg Abbott, TxDOT has suspended issuing approvals for Flock cameras or similar devices installed by third parties in our ROW [public roadways],” the spokesperson continued. 

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) ordered all state agencies in August to halt funding for Flock cameras. Nearly all Flock cameras in the state are purchased by cities through federal funding.

The concern spread to Florida which moved to halt the use of Flock cameras on state highways earlier this year. The Sunshine State’s Department of Transportation cited “concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life.”

Flock has a system of license plate readers, video cameras and audio detection devices incorporated into its AI database — logging details on a vehicle to make a “signature.”

Local jurisdictions can share collected data with other law enforcement agencies, creating a major network that can be used in crime solving, but has also led to misuse by officers in different agencies.

Within the last month, a detective in Deer Park, Texas, was suspended for using Flock’s system to search license plates over 150 times that were not related to any investigation, according to an ABC affiliate station.

Flock has attempted to combat this with new privacy guidelines issued in August that included adding more methods to detect suspicious searches.

Pushback to the AI vehicle surveillance systems has grown on both sides of the aisle, but has divided key figures within the GOP.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) stated that he’s worried ALPRs would turn the state into a “digital AI surveillance state where everything we’re doing is being tracked at all times.”

President Trump did not reflect similar concerns, however, telling reporters he liked the technology when asked about his thoughts on Flock cameras helping law enforcement stop crime.

“No, I sort of like them because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president said, adding later, “I like them.”

Flock did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

data.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror believed she was guilty 'from day one,' didn't have any doubts
data.description:
(NewsNation) — The lone juror whose vote resulted in a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder case says statements made about him by other jurors are not accurate.

Jury foreperson Roni Carlson told NBC 10 Boston that the holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, “admitted he had reasonable doubt” but allegedly refused to engage with the other jurors as to why. Carlson believed Desronvil was not properly applying the judge’s instructions on reasonable doubt and sent the judge a note raising her concerns.

Other jurors also alleged that Desronvil was dismissive of their arguments.

In a statement to NewsNation, he refuted the claims made by fellow jurors.

“I didn’t have any doubts,” the juror said. “As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present. Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned.”

Desronvil also spoke Tuesday in an interview with Ray Marcel on the streaming series “Fugitive TV.” Marcel told NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo on Wednesday that the lone juror believed Clancy was guilty from the beginning of the trial.

“He felt that she was sane when she did it. And that’s exactly what he told me,” Marcel recalled. “He said, from day one, that he always felt that she was guilty, and he never displayed or said anything about reasonable doubt.”

“He said things got heated in the jury room,” he continued. “Jurors were not agreeing, some agreeing, some not agreeing…. What he told me was, from day one, they voted every single day.”

Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, asked Judge William Sullivan to remove Desronvil from the jury, arguing that he was not following the law regarding reasonable doubt. The judge denied the request, and deliberations continued.

Holdout juror: Clancy prepared before kids’ deaths

Desronvil said that on the first day of deliberations, eight jurors believed Clancy was not guilty by reason of insanity.

By the end, only he and one other juror still believed she was guilty.

“And then, he said, at the last moment, that other juror decided to go not guilty, and he just stood his ground… He felt that she was sane by the preparation she did,” Marcel explained. “The preparation showed that she was sane and knew what she was doing, pretty much knew right from wrong, before she did what she did.”

He added that the public reaction after the trial was unreasonable. Since the mistrial, Desronvil has been publicly revealed as the holdout juror, had his address and phone number doxxed, and has received death threats.

Edward Andrew Paltzik, a leading defamation and media law attorney, announced Thursday that he is representing Desronvil.

“No matter if you agree with him or not… his name shouldn’t have been put out there like that,” Marcel told Cuomo. “No juror should be put to the forefront like that, because it’s their civic duty to do that, and they should be protected… He never asked for any of this whatsoever.”

NewsNation’s Steph Whiteside and Allison Hope Weiner contributed to this article.

data.title: Live updates: Trump sets up Medicaid drug price reductions; Vance stumps in Iowa with blistering attack on Dems
data.description:
The Midwest is home to several contentious congressional and gubernatorial races in November, historically red areas that are seeing Democratic candidates make inroads.

Vice President Vance visited one of them for a rally on Friday: Council Bluffs, Iowa. He was joined by Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who is running against Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand. Vance laid into Sand for more than five minutes at the rally.

The rally’s location is the turf of Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek, who is campaigning against Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) for the open seat. Hinson reportedly won’t attend the Vance event.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton (D) narrowly leads Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in a tight race for Senate, according a The Hill/Emerson College poll out Friday. It found Hamilton ahead by 2 percentage points, with 45 percent support to Marshall’s 43 percent.

The Pentagon told congressional leaders this week that the cost of the Iran war through Sept. 3 had exceeded $43 billion, not including damage estimates to sites hit.

At the White House, President Trump will make an announcement about Medicaid drug prices Friday afternoon. He’ll hold other meetings and will head Friday evening to his golf course in Sterling, Va., for a MAGA Inc. meeting. He’ll spend part of the weekend at Camp David.

Follow live below.

data.title: Wendy's franchisee with hundreds of locations across 15 states files for bankruptcy
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – A Wendy’s franchisee that operates 314 of the fast food company’s restaurants in 15 states announced Friday that it will be filing for bankruptcy.

Meritage Hospitality Group, headquartered in Grand Rapids, Michigan, announced in a news release that it was voluntarily filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in a bid to, in part, “strengthen its balance sheet.”

The news comes months after the company announced it would close 60 locations to boost its performance in 2026.

Meritage also owns one Bojangles and five “independently branded concepts,” but those ventures were not enough to offset the financial struggles of its Wendy’s stores.

“Because the substantial majority of Meritage’s restaurant portfolio operates under Wendy’s brand, those system-wide pressures have had a significant impact on the Company’s financial position,” the company said in the release.

Amid soaring beef costs, Wendy’s has reported same-store sales losses for six straight quarters, CNBC reports.

Meritage owns Wendy’s locations in Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia.

The company, which made no mention of any closure plans, says it anticipates maintaining normal restaurant operations during the restructuring process, and “will continue to serve guests every day, and its team members remain the heart of this business.”

Nexstar reached out to Wendy’s corporate team for a statement, but did not immediately receive a response.

data.title: 43 percent say Trump responsible for current state of economy: Survey
data.description:
A large share of Americans say President Trump is to blame for the current economic conditions facing the nation, including high inflation and affordability concerns, according to a new survey.

The Politico/Public First poll, released Thursday, found that 43 percent of respondents believe the president is mostly or fully responsible for the state of the economy. The survey indicated a deep partisan split on the issue, with 19 percent of Republicans and 70 percent of Democrats holding Trump accountable.

Meanwhile, another 16 percent said they place equal blame on Trump and former President Biden, while 29 percent placed greater blame on the latter.

A majority of Americans in this survey rated concerns about the cost of living as the top issue facing the U.S. right now. About 27 percent ranked the “poor state” of the economy and 22 percent selected high taxes as the nation’s top problem. 

This new data comes as the Trump administration seeks to calm concerns about affordability ahead of the midterms and amid ongoing U.S. military operations against Iran, which have strained global energy supplies, and a tariff fight with Canada. 

The president has repeatedly blamed unfavorable economic reports on the Biden administration and claimed energy prices that have skyrocketed during the Iran war “will drop precipitously” when the monthslong conflict comes to a close. 

During a Wednesday campaign event in North Carolina, Trump told supporters that higher gas prices were a “very inexpensive price to pay” for these military operations. 

This week, regular unleaded gas jumped from a national average of $4.31 to $4.43 in the span of four days, according to AAA. The national average price of diesel jumped by 42 cents over the last week.  

The Politico poll was conducted from Sept. 13-15 across a sample of 2,064 Americans. The margin of error is around 2.2 percentage points.

data.title: Silicon Valley Bank failure review finds Fed staff 'should have known' about risks
data.description:
A new review of the Silicon Valley Bank collapse found Federal Reserve supervisory staff “knew or should have known” about the institution’s vulnerabilities, Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said Friday.

The initial findings from an outside consulting firm’s independent review suggested the biggest bank failure since the 2008 financial crisis resulted from poor management and a lack of “decisive action” by Fed supervisory staff.

It also determined that a 2018 law rolling back portions of the Dodd-Frank Act did not contribute to the central bank’s delayed response, breaking with a prior assessment from Bowman’s predecessor.

“Their report marks a pivotal moment not just in our understanding of what went wrong at SVB, but in our understanding of what went wrong within the Federal Reserve’s supervisory process,” Bowman said in prepared remarks from London.

“This review is not about assigning blame,” she added. “Instead, it is about learning lessons from the past to avoid repeating them in the future.”

Bowman asked the Starling Advisory Group to conduct a new investigation into the bank’s failure after she took over as vice chair for supervision last June.

They found that Silicon Valley Bank’s collapse in early 2023, which was quickly followed by the failures of both First Republic Bank and Signature Bank, was the result of a “confluence of vulnerabilities.”

The bank faced unrealized losses as the Fed hiked interest rates in 2022 and 2023, according to the review. Its reliance on uninsured deposits from venture capital-backed tech firms compounded the problem and left it at risk of a run.

Fed supervisory staff “knew, or should have known, about these vulnerabilities as early as March 2022” and failed to take “prompt and decisive action to encourage or require” the bank to reduce its risks, the review noted.

It added that delays in supervisory action were not the result of “the regulatory tailoring mandate” in a 2018 law that loosened key portions of the Dodd-Frank Act, which was passed in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.

The review pointed to a “long-standing culture of risk aversion” among staff, who “believed it was personally safer to take no action unless they were certain the action was exactly right,” as well as confusion over who could decide on the right course of action.

Bowman’s predecessor, Michael Barr, issued an initial report on Silicon Valley Bank’s collapse in April 2023.

Barr, who still serves on the Fed board, similarly found that bank leaders failed to manage risks — while Fed supervisors did not “fully appreciate the extent” of the bank’s vulnerabilities or take sufficient steps to address these issues once they were identified.

However, his report also suggested that the 2018 rollback of portions of Dodd-Frank “impeded effective supervision by reducing standards, increasing complexity, and promoting a less assertive supervisory approach.”

data.title: Vance ends Iowa rally with seven-minute censure of Rob Sand
data.description:
Vice President Vance zeroed in on Iowa Democratic nominee Rob Sand during a rally in Council Bluffs on Friday, saying he is too far left to lead the state.

Rand is leading in several polls in the contest to succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) in November. 

In a roughly seven-minute attack on Sand, Vance accused Sand of masquerading as a moderate when he is “far left.” 

“He wants to make sure you hear him groaning about partisanship,” Vance told a crowd of supporters. 

“He’ll say ‘why do we even need labels,’ that’s what he says. But it’s a strange thing to complain about from a guy who has spent his entire life working for and donating to far left, Democratic causes. If partisanship is a problem, and it is, the first place is to look in the damn mirror, Rob, because you’ve been a partisan Democrat your whole life,” he said. 

Vance went on to hit Sand, who is the state’s auditor, on a number of fronts including transgender individuals in women’s sports, abortion, and the Green New Deal, and sought to paint he and other Democratic candidates as extreme. 

“The choice is this simple. It’s common sense versus crazy. It’s a man who listens to you versus a man who looks down on you. It’s a governor who fights for you versus a governor who fights against you,” Vance said. 

“You have an opportunity to not send not just Rob Sand but the entire Democrat Party a message: check the crazy at the door, and learn to fight for Americans for a change,” he continued. 

Polls show a tight gubernatorial race potentially favoring Democrats in the Hawkeye State. A poll released earlier this month from Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media shows Sand leading his Republican opponent Zach Lahn 49 to 46 percent. 

Vance notably called out Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton, along with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at the rally. The comments come as polls show a tightening Senate race in Kansas. 

While Lahn was present at the rally with Vance, one Iowa candidate who was noticeably absent  was Republican Senate nominee and Rep. Ashley Hinson.

The congresswoman’s Senate campaign said ahead of the rally that she had conflicting events. Hinson is facing a highly competitive race against Iowa State Rep. Josh Turek. The same Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media survey showed Turek leading Hinson 46 to 44 percent. 

Still, Vance gave Hinson a shoutout. 

“I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson for United States Senator from the great state of Iowa?” the vice president said.
